kurz: How Social Security is financed from payroll taxes, how the benefit is calculated from your earnings record and claiming age, and how to read your Social Security Statement.

bloecke.md:
Social Security, officially Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI), works largely on a pay-as-you-go basis. The payroll taxes that workers and employers pay this month are used to pay this month's benefits. Surpluses from earlier decades were invested in special-issue Treasury securities held in two trust funds. Since 2021, total costs have exceeded total income, including interest, so the reserves are shrinking.

There is no personal account in which your taxes are held and earn interest. With your payroll taxes, you earn credits and build an earnings record. The benefit is calculated from that record using a formula set in law. Today's workers finance today's retirees and in return acquire a claim that depends on future workers and on Congress. The Supreme Court held in Flemming v. Nestor (1960) that there is no contractual right to benefits; Congress can change the rules.

bloecke.titel: How the 12.4% Social Security tax is split in 2026
bloecke.unter: The tax on wages up to $184,500 goes to two trust funds. Medicare tax of 2.9% comes on top and finances hospital insurance, not Social Security.

bloecke.md: The payroll taxes are not invested for you; they pay current benefits. Instead of capital, you acquire an entitlement calculated from your lifetime earnings, financed by future payroll taxes, the remaining trust fund reserves and income tax on benefits.

## Credits and the taxable maximum

To qualify for retirement benefits, you need 40 credits. In 2026, you earn one credit for each $1,890 of wages or self-employment income, up to four credits a year. Ten years of work are therefore usually enough to qualify, but not for a high benefit.

Only earnings up to the taxable maximum count. In 2026 it is $184,500. Above it, no Social Security tax is due and no further benefits are earned. Both amounts rise every year with the national average wage index. The tax rate of 6.2% each for employee and employer has applied since 1990, apart from a temporary cut for employees in 2011 and 2012.

bloecke.formel: PIA = 90% × AIME up to $1,286 + 32% × AIME from $1,286 to $7,749 + 15% × AIME above $7,749
bloecke.erklaerung: The primary insurance amount (PIA) is the monthly benefit at full retirement age. It is calculated in two steps. First, your earnings in each year are indexed to wage growth up to the year you turn 60, and the 35 highest years are averaged per month. The result is the average indexed monthly earnings (AIME). Then the benefit formula with two bend points is applied. The bend points shown apply to people who turn 62 in 2026. From age 62, the PIA rises with every cost-of-living adjustment.

bloecke.beispiel: AIME of $5,820 (a career at the national average wage): 0.90 × $1,286 + 0.32 × $4,534 = $1,157.40 + $1,450.88 = $2,608.20 a month at full retirement age, in 2026 dollars

bloecke.md:
## The cost-of-living adjustment

Once benefits start, they rise each January with the cost-of-living adjustment (COLA). It equals the increase in the consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers (CPI-W) from the third quarter of the previous year to the third quarter of the current year. For 2026, it is 2.8%. If prices do not rise, there is no COLA, but benefits are never cut. That happened in 2016, after the fall in energy prices.

The COLA protects the [[Purchasing power|purchasing power]] of the benefit as measured by the CPI-W. Whether it keeps pace with the costs that matter most to retirees, such as health care and housing, is disputed. Part of each increase can also be absorbed by a rising Medicare Part B premium.

bloecke.titel: Cost-of-living adjustment by year in which it is paid
bloecke.unter: The COLA follows inflation with a lag: the high inflation of 2022 shows up in the 8.7% increase for 2023, the largest in four decades.

bloecke.md:
## Progressive by design

The three-step formula makes Social Security progressive. The first dollars of average monthly earnings are replaced at 90%, the next at 32% and the highest at only 15%. A low earner therefore receives a larger share of former pay than a high earner, even though the high earner receives the larger benefit in dollars. The table shows this for careers with 35 years at a constant ratio to the national average wage index of 2024, $69,846.08.

bloecke.titel: Earnings and benefit at full retirement age for someone turning 62 in 2026 (illustrative calculation)

bloecke.md: The replacement rate here is the PIA divided by monthly indexed earnings. It falls from 57.6% for the low earner to 32.7% at twice the average wage. Above the taxable maximum it falls further, because additional earnings no longer count. The figures assume 35 full years. Anyone with fewer years has zeros in the average and a lower benefit. For someone who reaches full retirement age in 2026 and always earned at least the taxable maximum, the Social Security Administration states a maximum benefit of $4,152 a month.

- The benefit is not based on your last salary or your best five years, but on your 35 highest years of indexed earnings.
- Full retirement age is not 65. For everyone born in 1960 or later, it is 67.
- The estimate in your statement is not guaranteed. It assumes that you keep earning about what you earn now until you claim, and that the law does not change.
- The gross benefit is not what reaches your bank account. Medicare premiums and, depending on income, federal income tax come off.

bloecke.md:
## Claiming age, reductions and delayed credits

Full retirement age (FRA) has risen gradually from 65. It is 66 for those born from 1943 to 1954, then rises by two months per birth year and reaches 67 for everyone born in 1960 or later. You can claim retirement benefits from 62 at the earliest.

If you claim early, the benefit is reduced by 5/9 of 1% for each of the first 36 months before FRA and by 5/12 of 1% for each additional month. With an FRA of 67, claiming at 62 cuts the benefit by 30%. The reduction is permanent. If you delay beyond FRA, you earn delayed retirement credits of 2/3 of 1% a month, 8% a year, up to age 70. There is no further increase after 70.

A spouse can receive up to 50% of the worker's PIA at the spouse's own FRA. A surviving spouse can receive up to 100% of what the deceased worker was receiving or was entitled to, including delayed credits.

bloecke.titel: Monthly benefit from a PIA of $2,608 at nine claiming ages (illustrative calculation)
bloecke.unter: Only the claiming age changes; additional earnings from working longer are not included. Between claiming at 62 and at 70 there is a difference of $1,408 a month for life, in 2026 dollars.

bloecke.md:
If you claim before FRA and keep working, the earnings test applies. In 2026, $1 of benefits is withheld for every $2 of earnings above $24,480. In the calendar year in which you reach FRA, $1 is withheld for every $3 above $65,160, counting only earnings before the month you reach FRA. Someone aged 63 who claims and earns $34,480 has $5,000 of benefits withheld.

The withheld money is not lost. At FRA, the benefit is recalculated so that months with withheld benefits no longer count as early months. From FRA onwards, you can earn any amount without withholding. Many people still do not know this and claim at 62 while working, only to see much of the first year's benefits withheld.

In a married couple, the higher earner's claiming age determines the survivor benefit for the rest of the surviving spouse's life. If the higher earner delays to 70, the survivor benefit is 24% higher than with a claim at 67. After a claim at 62, a survivor at full retirement age receives the larger of the reduced benefit and 82.5% of the PIA, so waiting until 70 still means around 50% more, because 1.24 / 0.825 = 1.50. This argument for delaying often carries more weight than the higher earner's own life expectancy.

## Your Social Security Statement

You can view your Social Security Statement at any time in a my Social Security account at ssa.gov. The Social Security Administration mails paper statements mainly to older workers who do not have an online account. The statement contains your earnings record and several estimates that are often confused.

schritte.text: Your earnings subject to Social Security tax for each year, as reported by employers and the IRS. It is the only part of the statement that involves no assumption.
Monthly estimates for each claiming age from 62 to 70 in today's dollars. They assume that you keep earning about your recent level until you claim.

The benefit you would receive now if you became unable to do substantial work for at least a year or had a condition expected to result in death. Disability benefits require recent work as well as total credits.
Estimates of what your spouse and minor children would receive if you died this year. They show what part of your family's income Social Security would replace.

bloecke.md: The estimates are only correct if the earnings record is complete. Look for years with zero or unusually low earnings, for example after a job change or from self-employment. You can ask the Social Security Administration to correct an error with Form SSA-7008 and evidence such as W-2 forms or tax returns. Correcting an error is easiest soon after it happens, while the documents are still available.

## Deductions from the gross benefit

If you are enrolled in Medicare Part B, the premium is usually deducted from your benefit. In 2026, the standard premium is $202.90 a month. Higher incomes pay an income-related monthly adjustment amount (IRMAA), based on the tax return from two years earlier. Part D drug coverage or a Medicare Advantage plan can cost more.

Federal income tax is then due, depending on income. Provisional income is your adjusted gross income without Social Security, plus tax-exempt interest, plus half of your benefits. Above $25,000 for single filers and $32,000 for joint filers, up to 50% of benefits become taxable, and above $34,000 or $44,000 up to 85% (26 U.S.C. § 86). These thresholds have never been indexed to inflation, so a growing share of retirees pays tax on benefits. You can have tax withheld from benefits with Form W-4V. Most states do not tax Social Security benefits; a few do.

bloecke.titel: Average-earner benefit before and after the Medicare Part B premium (2026)
bloecke.unter: Around $203 goes to the standard Part B premium; federal income tax is not yet taken into account.

bloecke.md: A single retiree receives $2,608.20 a month, $31,298 a year, and withdraws $20,000 from a Traditional IRA. Provisional income is $20,000 + $15,649 = $35,649. That is above $34,000, so 85% of the excess, $1,402, plus $4,500 becomes taxable: $5,902 of the benefits. Adjusted gross income is about $25,902. After the standard deduction of $16,100 and the temporary senior deduction of $6,000 for 2025 to 2028, less than $4,000 of taxable income remains even before the extra standard deduction for people 65 and older. The federal tax is a few hundred dollars at most. Larger withdrawals quickly make more of the benefits taxable.

bloecke.formel: Retirement gap = Spending need in retirement − (Social Security after Medicare premium and tax + other net income)
bloecke.erklaerung: All quantities are stated in today's dollars. The Social Security estimate in your statement is already in today's dollars, and the COLA keeps the benefit roughly constant in purchasing power. Other income such as a pension without inflation adjustment loses value over time and should be counted cautiously.
bloecke.beispiel: $4,000 need − $2,397 Social Security after Part B = $1,603 gap a month

bloecke.md:
A 45-year-old earns $75,000 a year. Her statement estimates a benefit of $2,600 a month at 67 in today's dollars.

1. Subtract the Medicare Part B standard premium: $2,600 − $202.90 = $2,397.10.
2. Assume a spending need of $4,000 a month in today's dollars.
3. The gap is $4,000 − $2,397.10 = $1,602.90 a month, that is $19,234.80 a year.
4. Over 25 years of retirement, the gap adds up to around $481,000 without interest.

Income tax on the benefit has not been deducted. The estimate also assumes that she keeps earning at her current level relative to the average wage until 67. Years of part-time work or a career break lower it. If you want to be cautious about the trust fund outlook, you can also calculate a variant with 80% of the estimated benefit.

Since January 2025, the Social Security Fairness Act has applied. It repealed the Windfall Elimination Provision and the Government Pension Offset, which had reduced benefits for people with a pension from work not covered by Social Security. Benefits were recalculated retroactively to January 2024.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act of July 2025 did not make Social Security tax-free. It introduced a temporary additional deduction of $6,000 for people aged 65 or older for 2025 to 2028, which lowers tax on all income, including taxable benefits. Measures to close the long-term financing gap, such as raising the taxable maximum, raising the full retirement age or changing the COLA formula, are being discussed but are not law.

mitnehmen: Social Security is an entitlement calculated from your earnings record and not an account balance; its value depends on future payroll taxes and on Congress.
The benefit at full retirement age (PIA) results from your 35 highest years of indexed earnings and a progressive formula that replaces 90%, 32% and 15% of three slices of average monthly earnings.
Low earners receive a larger share of their former pay than high earners; earnings above the taxable maximum of $184,500 (2026) do not count.
Claiming at 62 cuts the benefit by 30% for life with an FRA of 67, and each year of delay up to 70 adds 8%; the higher earner's choice also sets the survivor benefit.
Calculate your gap in today's dollars, with the benefit after the Medicare premium and income tax, not with the gross figure in your statement.

begriffe.text: Your 35 highest years of earnings up to the taxable maximum, indexed to wage growth up to the year you turn 60, divided by 420 months. Years without earnings count as zero.

The monthly Social Security benefit at full retirement age, calculated from the AIME with the progressive formula of 90%, 32% and 15%. Early or delayed claiming and spouse or survivor benefits are derived from it.
The age at which you receive 100% of your PIA. It is 66 for those born from 1943 to 1954 and rises in steps of two months to 67 for those born in 1960 or later.
Annual increase of Social Security benefits each January in line with the CPI-W from the third quarter of the previous year. It was 2.8% for 2026; if prices fall, benefits stay the same.
The highest amount of annual earnings subject to Social Security tax and counted for benefits; $184,500 in 2026. It rises each year with the national average wage index.
Increase of the benefit for each month you claim after full retirement age, 2/3 of 1% a month or 8% a year for those born in 1943 or later, up to age 70.
